name: Depend on a relay
summary: The unit works only while a friendly relay stands and has power: a control building, a beacon or a commander unit. If the relay is destroyed, captured or starved of power, every unit tied to it shuts down where it is, unable to move or fire, and one hovering over water sinks; the units come back to life once a working relay exists again. The relay pays for something the unit could not otherwise have at its price, such as no driver to mind-control, a power-hungry weapon or a body that is hard to kill, and turns that strength into a single point of failure the enemy can hunt. The levers are how many relays there are, whether one covers the whole map or only a radius, how long a shutdown lasts and how quickly a spare can be built.
counterplay: Find and destroy the relay: it is usually softer and easier to reach than the units it runs, and losing it switches all of them off at once.
Cut its power instead: raid the power plants or the supply that feed it, or black it out with a spy or a saboteur (in Red Alert 2 a Spy in a power plant shuts the grid down for a while).
Capture it with an engineer where the game allows; Red Alert 2 robot tanks also shut down when their control center is captured or sold.
Time the relay kill with your push so the shut-down units are free kills, and catch hovering units over water when it falls.
Raid it from an unexpected side: the owner can't guard the relay and fight at the front with the same units.
Watch for the spare: the owner protects the relay or builds a backup, so hit both, or hit the new one while it is still going up.

other_examples.unit: Base power, the Robot Control Center and the Spy's blackout (Yuri's Revenge)
other_examples.note: Robot Tanks and their control center both stop on low or no power, and an Allied Spy who gets into an enemy power structure shuts that side's power off for a while, so a raid on the grid can switch the robots off without touching the center. In the engine a flag on the center ties the tanks to it: they are switched off whenever their owner has no working, powered center left and switched back on by the next one, though the logic breaks down when one side owns more than one kind of such building. Across the series the same grid runs the top-tier base defences, which also go dark in a blackout, so striking the power plants is a standard way to leave a base blind and helpless.

sources.title: Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 - Yuri's Revenge manual (transcript), Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Copies the Yuri's Revenge manual: the Robot Tank and Robot Control Center entries and the Spy's effect on each enemy building.

sources.title: PowersUnit, ModEnc
sources.note: The Yuri's Revenge rules flag behind the Robot Control Center link, with its known limitations.

other_examples.unit: Laser Tank (USA Laser General, Zero Hour)
other_examples.note: Its laser needs more power than the tank itself can make, so power is beamed to it from the base grid, and each tank takes up one unit of the base's power. When the base runs short, every Laser Tank goes inactive along with the base defences, so destroying the general's power plants disarms his tank army; its infobox flags the dependence on power.

other_examples.unit: Novax Center and Novax Defense Satellite (UEF, Forged Alliance)
other_examples.note: The satellite can't be harmed by anything short of a nuke, but losing its ground center switches it off and sends it crashing down, at times onto its own target. The wiki's advice to the victim is simply to attack the center, and to the owner to protect it: an untouchable unit with a breakable relay.

sources.title: UEF Experimental Satellite System, Supreme Commander Wiki

other_examples.note: Protoss buildings run on the power field of a nearby pylon: in the original game a building that loses the field stops working until a pylon covers it again, and in StarCraft II units from warp gates are warped in inside a field. A pylon placed far forward, a proxy pylon, lets an army reinforce near the enemy, and a Warp Prism can stand in as a mobile power source when a pylon falls. Here the relay powers buildings and reinforcements rather than units already in the field.

sources.title: Pylon, StarCraft Wiki
sources.version: StarCraft and StarCraft II: Legacy of the Void

other_examples.unit: Airfield and its plane (Yak and MiG)
other_examples.note: Each Airfield supports one plane, which lands there to reload after every attack. If the Airfield is destroyed while its plane is in the air, the plane crashes: a home-pad relay whose loss kills rather than pauses.

sources.title: Airfield (Red Alert 1), Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Its quote box copies the Red Alert manual's Airfield entry, which states the one-plane rule and the crash.

other_examples.note: For contrast (belongs to the launch-drones pattern): a drone bought for a vehicle follows it and is destroyed with it, and also when the vehicle loses its crew to a sniper's crew kill or to neutron weapons. A host-unit relay in miniature, though the drone is an add-on rather than a unit a player would control.

shooter_analogues.note: In this Marines-against-aliens team shooter, every Marine structure in a room runs on that room's power node. If the aliens destroy the node, the room's structures go dead until power is restored: spawn portals stop bringing Marines back, armories stop handing out health and ammo, research in progress is cancelled, and the arms lab's weapon and armour upgrades are lost at once. Sentries need a battery placed near them instead, which works without room power. The wiki tells Marines to defend nodes at all costs and aliens to hit the node rather than each structure.

sources.title: Power Nodes (Natural Selection 2), Natural Selection Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: A player-built base runs on its silo: modules inside the silo's radius draw power from its cortium stock, modules out of range or left without a silo decay and self-destruct, and a silo that runs dry loses health and blows up. Mining trucks (ANTs) have to keep bringing cortium in, so a long siege that keeps the trucks away can starve a base as surely as an attack on the silo.

Each of the commander's resources except the supply and vehicle drops is tied to a physical asset on the map that must be working before it can be used. Special Forces players destroy the assets with C4 and other explosives, and Engineers repair them with the wrench or a supply drop, so the commander's tools become objectives for both teams. In Battlefield 4 the main assets depend on holding control points instead.

player_translation.summary: A cheap or unusually strong unit that runs on a team relay: a control station the team builds or the map provides, a beacon a teammate plants, or a command unit. While the relay stands, the unit outperforms its price; when the enemy destroys, captures or blacks out the relay, every linked unit gets a short warning and then shuts down where it is until a relay works again, with a way out for the player inside.
as_user: You buy a unit that is better than its tier suggests, such as a cheap hover tank that can't be mind-controlled or a light tank carrying a heavy laser, because part of it lives in the relay.
Your HUD always shows the relay's health, power and distance. When it comes under attack you get an alert and decide whether to go back and defend it or trust your team.
When it falls, a siren and a short reserve-power countdown give you time to reach cover, moving slowly and unable to fire; then you shut down. Your camera keeps working and you can still ping.
While shut down you either wait for the relay to be rebuilt and restart where you stand, or hold X to recall: you respawn as if you had died, but the enemy gets no kill reward.
A hovercraft over water sinks when it shuts down, so the warning tells you to make for land.
as_target: Linked enemies carry a small link icon that names their relay, so you know what they depend on; the relay itself shows on your map once someone has spotted it.
The best play is often to ignore the linked units and hit the relay: raid it with fast or stealthy units, shell it, capture it with an engineer, or cut the power that feeds it.
When it falls, the linked units go dark and can't move or fire for a while, which is your team's window to push past them or pick them off.
teammates: The relay's team has to guard and repair it (engineers, turrets, cover), keep its power supplied, and build a spare before the first one falls.
Players on linked units share one risk, so the team decides how many to field, and a relay can serve only so many units, as each Generals Laser Tank draws its own share of power.
The enemy team sends a raid group (an infiltrator, a raider, artillery with a spotter) and times the relay kill with its main push.
A relay carried by a teammate makes a protector pair: the carrier keeps the linked units alive simply by staying alive and in range.
controls: The base pattern is passive and spends no counted key; the relay widget sits on the HUD.
Middle mouse, the universal ping, on your relay: 'defend the relay'; on an enemy relay: 'attack the relay'.
While shut down, hold X to recall: respawn at once, with no kill reward for the enemy.
The carried-beacon variant puts 'plant or pick up the beacon' on Q, one counted key within the T1 budget.
feedback: A thin link line from each linked unit to its relay for its own team, and a link icon over the unit that everyone can see.
Alerts: 'relay under attack', 'relay lost, shutdown in a few seconds' with a siren, and 'relay restored'.
Shut-down units go dark: lights off, a power-down sound, a grey model and an 'offline' icon both teams can read.
Restart: a power-up sound and a reboot ring that fills before the unit can fire again.
Field variants draw the relay's radius on the ground and warn a linked unit as it nears the edge.
changes_from_rts: Red Alert 2's shutdown is instant and lasts until a powered control center is rebuilt, however long that takes. A player needs a warning, a short reserve-power window and a way out (recall), or one relay kill leaves people idle for minutes.

In Red Alert 2 the control center sits in a base the player builds; in a shooter the relay has to stand on the map, reachable, marked once spotted and rebuildable, so that killing or saving it becomes a team objective.

Red Alert 2 switches all of a player's robot tanks off together once no powered control center is left; here relays belong to the team, there can be several, and each serves a limited number of units, so one loss doesn't switch off the whole team.
Base power (the Red Alert 2 low-power rule, the Generals power grid) becomes a relay power meter fed by objectives or supply runs, or is dropped for a simple standing-or-destroyed rule.
Sinking over water kills outright; keep it to the hover class with a long warning, as a high-spice variant.
The robot tank's strength (no driver to mind-control) comes with the pattern as its paired strength, so the drawback always buys something.

team_play.notes: The relay is an objective for both teams: its owners must guard, power and replace it, the enemy must find, raid or black it out, and linked players depend on teammates they may never see.

notes: The relay is an entity with health, power and an owner; linked units read its state from the server.
Shutdown and restart states must stop movement, weapons and abilities everywhere, with a grace timer, the recall and sinking over water.
Relays have to fit the maps and modes: who places them, where, how they are rebuilt and how they show on both teams' maps.
Several relays, capacity limits and capture rules add edge cases; ModEnc notes that Red Alert 2's own logic misbehaves when one side owns more than one kind of powering building.
UI: the HUD widget, link icons, alerts and offline states.
One relay kill can switch off several players at once, a big swing that can decide a match.
Players who sit shut down for long stop playing; keep shutdowns short and the recall free.
If the relay is too safe the drawback vanishes and the linked unit is simply underpriced; if it is too exposed, nobody buys the unit.
Relay camping: a team that sits on the enemy's relay site can lock linked units out for good unless a spare can go up elsewhere.
Both teams must see which units depend on which relay, and where the relay is once it has been spotted.
A shut-down unit must look different from an EMP-disabled or frozen one, and show when it will restart.
Players must understand why they shut down, so the alert names the relay and the cause: destroyed, captured or out of power.

variants.name: Control station
variants.summary: One team building powers every linked unit anywhere on the map; destroying, capturing or unpowering it shuts them all down until it is rebuilt.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2: Yuri's Revenge Robot Tank and Robot Control Center

variants.name: Grid draw
variants.summary: Each linked unit draws a share of the team's power or supply; when the supply runs short, all linked units stop together, so raids on power plants or supply runs disarm them.
variants.seen_in: Generals Laser Tank (one unit of power per tank), the Red Alert 2 low-power rule, PlanetSide 2 Cortium Silo

variants.name: Power field
variants.summary: The unit works only inside the radius of a friendly pylon or beacon; leaving the field, or losing the pylon, shuts it down, and teammates can plant forward pylons to push the field.
variants.seen_in: StarCraft Protoss pylons, Natural Selection 2 power nodes (one per room), PlanetSide 2 silo radius

variants.name: Carried beacon
variants.summary: The unit plants its own relay beacon and works within its radius; to advance it must pick the beacon up and plant it again, and enemies who find the beacon can strand it.
variants.seen_in: An original twist: a one-unit version of StarCraft's proxy pylon and Warp Prism field

adds_strengths.why: Carries its own relay, so it fights above its price wherever it plants the beacon, with no base to defend.

adds_weaknesses.why: Shuts down whenever it leaves the beacon's radius or the beacon is destroyed, and has to stop to move it forward.

variants.name: Commander link
variants.summary: A teammate's command unit is the relay: linked units within its range work, and if the commander dies they shut down until it respawns or another commander comes close.
variants.seen_in: An original twist; Generals vehicle drones, which die with their parent vehicle, are a cousin

variants.name: Home pad
variants.summary: An aircraft tied to one landing pad where it reloads its limited ammo; if the pad is destroyed while the aircraft is flying, it crashes, or in a gentler version must glide to another pad.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 1 Airfield (one plane per airfield)

variants.name: Dead in the water
variants.summary: A hovercraft that loses its relay over water sinks and is lost, so its owner keeps to land whenever the relay is under threat.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2: Yuri's Revenge Robot Tank

variants.name: Untouchable, but tethered
variants.summary: The unit itself can't be harmed by ordinary weapons; it can be stopped only by destroying its relay, which also brings it down.
variants.seen_in: Supreme Commander: Forged Alliance Novax Defense Satellite

adds_strengths.why: Ordinary weapons can't harm it, so it keeps fighting until the enemy reaches its relay.

adds_weaknesses.why: Destroying its relay disables it at once and brings it down, so its whole life hangs on a structure the enemy can reach.

adds_strengths.why: Part of its power lives in the team's relay, so it fights above its price: cheaper, harder to kill or better armed than its tier suggests.

adds_weaknesses.why: Shuts down where it stands whenever its relay is destroyed, captured or unpowered, and stays helpless until a relay works again.

countered_by.why: Saboteurs and spies reach the relay or black out its power, switching off every linked unit at once.
Fast raiders slip past the front to hit the relay while its units are busy fighting.
Artillery shells the relay from beyond the fight.

open_questions: Where does the relay come from in Shamble Frontlines: a structure every team gets, a deployable another player buys, or a beacon the linked unit plants itself?
Does one relay serve the whole team or only the player who bought the linked unit, and how many units may it serve?
How long may a shutdown last before the player can recall, and should a recall cost anything?
Should the enemy always see the relay, or only once someone has spotted it?
Should a hovercraft over water really sink, or only stall until the relay returns?

shooter_fit.reason: It turns a support structure into a team objective, as Natural Selection 2's power nodes do, but being switched off by something across the map feels bad for the player inside, so it needs warnings, short shutdowns and a recall.
